Annual Meetings

Afternoon Session - 2011 Meeting

Warren Buffett tells shareholders a CEO should be left "dead broke" after a "too big to fail" bailout and warns Congress against what he thinks would be its most "asinine" act ever.

Sat, Apr 30 2011 • 1:00 PM EDT
Key Chapters —
  1. 6. CEO should be left "dead broke" after a bailout
  2. 15. Munger really loves Costco
  3. 23. Buffett: There shouldn't even be a debt ceiling
  4. 27. Buffett owns a few stocks and lots of bonds
  5. 32. Buffett's advice: invest in your own skills

6. CEO should be left "dead broke" after a bailout

WARREN BUFFETT: OK. Let's go to number 11.

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Getting too close to confession time up here. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

AUDIENCE MEMBER: Good afternoon, Warren and Charlie. My name is Phil Drew (PH), and I'm here with my wife Tina and our good friends the Grummys (PH) and the Henriksens (PH).

Sync Video to Paragraph

We're all from Indianapolis, and we're all small businesspeople. So we are not too big to fail.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And our question, basically, is simply this: do either of you gentlemen think that we might be headed down the same type of path years from now when we get into a situation as taxpayers, that we might have to bail out a company on Wall Street that is too big to fail? And if so, have we done anything to avert that?

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: There are institutions around the world that I think governments should properly â although people won't like it â but I think that there are institutions around the world that governments would properly â I think bailout has got a little bit of a pejorative term on it, in the sense that stockholders should not be saved, managers should not be saved â but certainly the institutions, in some cases, should not be allowed to collapse immediately.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I mean, right now, we're continuing to follow that policy, for example, with Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae. I mean, they have not reconstituted themselves, as many of the banks and the auto companies.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I mean, Chrysler is even paying back, which, you know, surprises me, but my hat is off to them, and I mean that sincerely. I was really on the fence on saving the auto companies, but I think the administration did the right thing.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I mean, there were â they weren't saving the auto companies, per se, they were still working at saving a very fragile economy.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And, like I say, particularly in retrospect, they certainly, in my view, made the right decision.

Sync Video to Paragraph

There are â right now, you know, in Europe they're deciding whether countries are too big to fail.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And so I think that problem will always be with us.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I think for that reason that you have to do things to reduce the propensity to fail, and among those things, I think you have to make it so that the CEO, and to some extent the board â but not to the draconian degree that I'll suggest for the CEO â I think that any institution that requires society to come and bail it out for society's sake should have a system in place that leaves their CEO, basically, and his spouse, dead broke, because I think that the upside and downside incentives are vastly different. (Applause)

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I think the board of directors of those institutions should suffer severe penalties. Nothing like that, but they certainly, you know, should give back, say, the last five years of directorsâ fees or whatever it may be that they received.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Because they â if you run an institution that actually needs â society can suffer such a blow if you fail â that society needs to come in and save you, you ought to have somebody running that institution, and you ought to have incentive practices in place that make it very, very, very painful to the people involved for the failure if it indeed happens.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And you also ought to reduce leverage in the system, and I think we've gone, to some degree, in that direction.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But there will be too big to fail institutions 10 years from now or 20 years from now. Right now Freddie Mac and Fanny Mae are sort of too big to figure out.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We just sit there â and incidentally, here's nothing wrong with that. It's more important to come up with the right solution than it is to come up with an immediate solution on those.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But particularly, I would say, in Europe there are banking institutions in countries that people are facing the question of whether they are too big to fail.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Charlie?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Well, my answer is that the past panics and depressions, by and large, started on Wall Street or in stock brokerages.

Sync Video to Paragraph

They tended to involve great waves of excessive speculation and bad behavior in the people who were profiting from those waves as salesman, or market makers, or promoters or what have you.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And I think that this last mess, which created so much danger, should have caused something like happened in the aftermath of the '30s, where we prevented a new mess for a long, long time, but, of course, it hasn't done that.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And so I think you can confidently expect a new mess or two before you career is over, and I think it is really stupid for our country to have allowed this.

Sync Video to Paragraph

Partly the failure is not one of evil, it's one of stupidity. And part of the stupidity is in our great academic institutions who believe a whole lot of things that aren't true. And that is a really hard problem to solve.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: You're talking about particularly in finance?

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yes, of course, and economics, too.

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: Yeah.

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Those are not hard sciences, finance and economics. And finance really attracts people who should have gone into snake charming or â (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

WARREN BUFFETT: If there's anybody we've forgotten to insult, just pass a note up, and we'll get to you. (Laughter)

Sync Video to Paragraph

CHARLIE MUNGER: Yeah.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And market conditions â you know, you heard Charlie in the movie talk about opportunity costs. Our opportunity costs were different in every single one of those five transactions. And incidentally, we could have done a much better â I could have done a much better â job of allocating our money, you know, in terms of the post-panic period.

Sync Video to Paragraph

I was early on Goldman and GE, compared to the situation five months later. But, you know, we don't have â we not only don't have perfect foresight, sometimes it's pretty bad.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But each deal â when I did the Swiss Re deal, I was not thinking about the Dow Chemical deal, which was committed to, maybe, a year-plus earlier. I was thinking about what else I could do with $2.7 billion, and that's the way all the decisions are made.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So they are not related â they're not related to each other. They go through a mind that is looking at everything available that day, including the amount of cash we have, the likelihood of being able to do something else next week or next month, what else we can do that day. And past deals we've made don't really make any difference.

Sync Video to Paragraph

In fact, one of the things â one of the errors people make in business â and sometimes it can be a huge error â is that they try and measure every deal against the best deal they've ever made.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So they say, you know, I made this wonderful deal for, maybe, an insurance policy written, or it might be a company bought, it might be a stock bought, and they're determined that they're never going to make a deal that isn't that attractive in the future.

So they, in effect â sometimes they take themselves out of the game.

Sync Video to Paragraph

The goal is not to make a better deal than you've ever made before. The goal is to make a satisfactory deal that's the best deal you can make at the time. And Charlie relates it to marriage, and I'll let him expand on that. (Laughter)

Ironically, he could well be right if it were in our determination, but just take our three major states in electric utility operation, where we serve almost two million customers, Iowa, Utah, and Oregon, but it's true of other states as well.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We operate under the dictates of the utility commissions in those three states, all of which â or each of which â sets their own rules regarding operation, and each of which we end up obeying.

Sync Video to Paragraph

If we were to unilaterally, for example, decide to close down significant coal generation, we would be told to depreciate those plants over a shorter period, and that would translate, not in the cost to Berkshire, it would translate into higher rates for electricity there.

Sync Video to Paragraph

We are entitled to a return on our investment and the faster the depreciation, the higher the rates have to be in order to achieve allowed returns.

Sync Video to Paragraph

So there was a woman from Oregon speaking, for example. And the burden of any unilateral attempt by us â and we couldnât do it without the approval of the utility commissions â but the burden would fall on customers.

Sync Video to Paragraph

And it is true, actually, that we would recoup accelerated depreciation and we would probably have a much larger investment on which we would be allowed a return in other generating facilities.

Sync Video to Paragraph

But this is a question â this is not something that the stockholders of Berkshire end up incurring the costs of. It's something that the rate, or the users of electricity in these various states, will pay for.
